Question_text: In this experiment, you will determine the mass of a metre rule using the principle of moments. You have been provided with: • a metre rule with a hole at the 1.0cm mark, • a knife-edge to act as a pivot in (a), • a rod held in a boss to act as a pivot in (b), • a pulley wheel held in a clamp and stand, • a length of string with two loops, • a mass and hook, labelled S, • a card showing m, the mass of S, • a half-metre rule, • a set square.

Parts.part_text: Balance the metre rule on the knife-edge and record the distance d of the centre of mass of the metre rule from the 0.0 cm mark on the rule.

Set up the apparatus shown in Fig. 1.1. Pass the rod through the hole at the 1.0cm mark on the rule. Place the loop at one end of the string over the rule at the 60.0cm mark on the rule. Place the string over the pulley and suspend the mass S from the loop at the other end of the string using the hook. Initially, end B of the metre rule rests on the bench. Move the loop along the metre rule towards end B. Keep the length PQ of the string vertical by moving the pulley horizontally. Eventually end B of the metre rule rises off the bench. Adjust the positions of the loop and the pulley to make the rule horizontal and the string PQ vertical.
Parts.image: A diagram (Fig. 1.1) shows a metre rule supported by a rod passing through a hole at the 1.0 cm mark, acting as a pivot. The rod is held by a boss on a stand. A string is attached to the metre rule at a distance 'y' from the pivot and passes over a pulley wheel, suspending a mass 'S'. The centre of mass of the rule is at a distance 'x' from the pivot. The rule is balanced horizontally over a bench surface, with the string PQ shown vertically.

Parts.part_text: Explain how you made sure that the string PQ is vertical. You may add to Fig. 1.1 if you wish.
the distance x from the centre of the rod to the centre of mass of the metre rule,
the distance y from the centre of the rod to the position of the string on the metre rule.
Calculate the mass M of the rule using the relationship M = my/x where m is the mass of S, and is written on the card.

Question_text: In this experiment, you will determine the time for one oscillation of a simple pendulum. You have been provided with: • a simple pendulum, • a metre rule, • a stopwatch, • a pin in a cork.

Parts.part_text: The apparatus shown in Fig. 2.1 has been set up for you. Measure the length l of the simple pendulum from the base of the split cork to the centre of the pendulum bob.
Parts.image: A diagram (Fig. 2.1) illustrates a simple pendulum setup. A stand, boss, and clamp hold a split cork. A string of length 'l' suspends a pendulum bob from the split cork. A pin in a cork is placed on the bench surface directly below the pendulum bob to mark its central position.

Parts.part_text: Place the pin so that it marks the central position of the pendulum bob when it is stationary, as shown in Fig. 2.1. When the pendulum bob is pulled to the side and released, it moves from side to side. One complete oscillation of the pendulum bob is from O to A to B and back to O, as shown in Fig. 2.2.
Parts.image: A diagram (Fig. 2.2) shows a pendulum bob oscillating. The central position is labelled O. The bob moves from O to an extreme position A, then through O to the other extreme position B, and finally back to O, illustrating one complete oscillation.

Parts.part_text: The time for 20 complete oscillations of the bob is t. Take measurements to determine an accurate value of t.
Calculate the time T for one oscillation.
Calculate a value for the acceleration of free fall g, using the relationship g = 4π²l/T². Give a unit for your answer.

Question_text: In this experiment, you will measure the critical angle for light in a transparent block. You have been provided with: • a semi-circular transparent block, • an illuminated slit, • a protractor.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 3.2 on page 7 of your question paper, draw a normal to the line XY at the point M, towards the bottom of the page. The length of the normal should be greater than the radius of the semi-circular block.
To the left of the normal draw a line at an angle of incidence of 60° to the normal. Label this line L. This line should also be longer than the radius of the block.

Place the semi-circular block on Fig. 3.2 of your question paper with the straight edge along line XY and with the centre of the straight edge at M. This is shown in Fig. 3.1. Arrange the light source and slit so that a ray of light passes along the line L. Draw around the semi-circular edge of the block.
Parts.image: A diagram (Fig. 3.1, not to scale) shows a semi-circular transparent block placed with its straight edge along a line XY, with its centre at point M. An incident ray of light, labelled 'line L', approaches the block from a slit, striking the straight edge at M. The emergent ray leaves the curved surface of the block.

Parts.part_text: Mark and label two points, P₁ and P₂, on the ray that leaves the block.
Remove the block. Draw a line connecting P₁ and P₂ and extend this line to meet XY.
Measure the angle of reflection.

Replace the block in its marked position on Fig. 3.2, with the light ray passing along the line L. Change the angle of incidence until light leaves the block at M as close as possible to the direction MY.
Parts.image: A diagram (Fig. 3.2) shows a horizontal line labelled XY with point M in the middle. This is a blank space provided for the student to draw the setup as per the instructions.

Parts.part_text: Mark and label two points P₃ and P₄ on the incident ray.
Remove the block. Draw a line connecting points P₃ and P₄ and extend this line to meet XY.
The new angle of incidence of the ray of light is approximately equal to the critical angle for light in the transparent block. Measure this angle of incidence.

Question_text: In this experiment, you will investigate the power transferred by a light-emitting diode (LED). You have been provided with an incomplete circuit consisting of: • a power supply, • an ammeter, • a voltmeter, • an LED, • a resistor labelled 'X', • a switch. You have also been provided with three resistors labelled with the values of their resistances and some additional connecting leads.

Parts.part_text: Connect the 68 Ω resistor between points A and B.
In the space below, draw a circuit diagram of the completed circuit.
Close the switch and record the potential difference V across the LED and the current I in the circuit. Open the switch.
Calculate the power P transferred by the LED using the relationship P = I V.

Replace the 68 Ω resistor first with the 180 Ω resistor and then with the 330 Ω resistor. Then use all possible series combinations of the 68 Ω, 180 Ω and 330 Ω resistors. In each case repeat (b) and (c). Record your results in a table in the space below. Include the results from (b) and (c) in the table. Include a column for the values of the resistors used in the gap between A and B.
Using the grid opposite, plot a graph of P/mW against I/mA. Draw the line of best fit.
Parts.image: A large blank grid is provided for plotting a graph, with space for labelling the axes and scales. It is intended for plotting P/mW against I/mA.

Parts.part_text: Determine the power transferred by the LED when the current in it is 10mA.
